title: Amplemarket AI Sales Tool Review: Where It Fits vs Research-First AI SDRs
summary: A fair Amplemarket AI sales tool review for B2B outbound teams. See where Amplemarket fits, where platform breadth stops, and when a research-first AI SDR like Coldreach is the better choice.
body_text: Amplemarket is not a lightweight cold email sender. It is also not just a contact database. Based on its official positioning, Amplemarket is an AI sales copilot for sales teams. The product surface spans intelligence, lead generation and signals, multichannel engagement, deliverability optimization, integrations, and several AI assistant surfaces under the Duo brand. That makes Amplemarket relevant for a specific kind of buyer: a team that wants to consolidate more of the outbound stack into one platform. If you are running separate tools for prospecting, enrichment, sequences, inbox management, intent signals, social workflows, voice, and deliverability checks, a broader platform can be attractive. But the buying decision should be more precise than “Do we need an AI sales tool?” Most outbound teams do not fail because they lack another place to send sequences. They fail because the outreach does not prove enough account understanding. The message says the recipient’s name, title, company, and maybe a generic trigger. It still does not answer the only question the buyer cares about: why are you contacting me, why now, and why should I believe this is relevant? That is the difference this Amplemarket review covers. Amplemarket may fit if your main goal is platform consolidation across prospecting, engagement, signals, AI assistance, inbox workflows, and deliverability utilities. A research-first AI SDR like Coldreach is a better fit if the core bottleneck is relevance, account qualification, and writing from evidence before any email goes out. Fast verdict: Amplemarket vs research-first AI SDRs Category Amplemarket Coldreach Best understood as AI sales copilot and engagement platform Research-first AI SDR Best for Stack consolidation across data, signals, sequences, inbox, voice, social workflows, and deliverability utilities Researched outbound where every lead is qualified before messaging Starting point Sales platform workflow: find leads, use signals, engage across channels Account truth: pain, status quo, and in-market evidence Messaging motion AI copy and assistant surfaces can support outreach workflows Outreach is written from lead-level research Official product surface used in this review Intelligence, Lead Generation & Signals, Multichannel Engagement, Deliverability Optimization, Integrations, Duo Copilot, Duo Copywriter, Duo Inbox, Duo Voice, Searcher, Intent Signals, Job Change Alerts, Competitive Intelligence, Social Prospecting, Data Enrichment, Email Validation, Multichannel Sequences, Unibox, Social Automation, Analytics, Workflows, Deliverability Booster, Mailbox Recommendation, Email Spam Checker AI SDR that researches, qualifies, writes, sends through customer infrastructure, monitors replies, and learns Public pricing snapshot Startup shown at $600/month on an annual term for 2 users and 27,000 contacts. Growth and Elite are custom Coldreach starts at $899/month Main buyer question “Can we consolidate more outbound workflow into one platform?” “Can we improve reply quality by starting from account evidence?” Choose when You want one broad platform for outbound execution and related utilities You need higher-quality replies from better account research and in-market reasoning What Amplemarket is Amplemarket’s homepage title, according to the official site reviewed on 2026-06-22, is “Amplemarket: AI Sales Copilot for sales teams.” Its pricing page is titled “Amplemarket: Platform Pricing.” That positioning matters. Amplemarket is not describing itself as only a sequencer. It is positioning as a sales copilot and platform. The official product navigation presents Amplemarket as a broad sales system. Listed product areas and modules include Intelligence, Lead Generation & Signals, Multichannel Engagement, Deliverability Optimization, Integrations, Duo Copilot, Duo Copywriter, Duo Inbox, Duo Voice, Searcher, Intent Signals, Job Change Alerts, Competitive Intelligence, Social Prospecting, Data Enrichment, Email Validation, Multichannel Sequences, Unibox, Social Automation, Analytics, Workflows, Deliverability Booster, Mailbox Recommendation, and Email Spam Checker. That is a large surface area. The promise is not only “send email.” It is closer to “run more of your outbound sales workflow from one place.” The official pricing snapshot supports that read. Amplemarket’s visible Startup plan is shown at $600/month on an annual term for small businesses, startups, and founder-led sales teams. It includes 2 users, 27,000 contacts, Scaled CSM, Community Onboarding, Multichannel Sequences, AI Intent Signals, and Duo Copilot. Growth is custom, with 4 users, 140,000 contacts, Dedicated CSM, Personalized Onboarding, Multichannel Sequences, AI Intent Signals, Duo Copilot, and Duo Voice. Elite is custom, with 10 users, 400,000 contacts, Dedicated CSM, Personalized Onboarding, Multichannel Sequences, AI Intent Signals, Duo Copilot, Duo Voice, and Duo Inbox. The strongest case for Amplemarket is simple: if you want to reduce tool sprawl, a consolidated platform can be easier to buy, train on, and manage than separate systems for data, enrichment, engagement, AI copy, inbox workflows, voice, and deliverability checks. Amplemarket’s own site includes this customer quote: “By cutting licenses and consolidating into Amplemarket, we cut tooling costs by about 56%.” - Thanbir Moktadir, Director of Global Account Development. That quote captures the platform’s clearest buyer promise: consolidation. Where Amplemarket fits Amplemarket makes the most sense for teams that want a broad sales engagement and copilot platform in one place. A team might evaluate Amplemarket if it wants multichannel engagement, lead generation and signals, data enrichment, email validation, AI assistance across copy and sales workflows, inbox tools, voice, social automation, and deliverability utilities in one commercial relationship. That is a real use case. Bad data creates waste before the first message is sent. Poor deliverability means strong copy may never be seen. Disconnected inbox and sequence workflows make follow-up harder to manage. Separate enrichment, validation, and engagement systems can create operational drag. For teams with those problems, consolidation is a rational buying motion. This is especially true when the team’s outbound program already has clear messaging, clear ICP boundaries, and clear buying triggers. In that case, the bottleneck may be operational execution: managing contact data, coordinating channels, reducing tool overlap, keeping deliverability checks close to sending workflows, and helping reps move faster. None of that is a criticism. It is a valid platform strategy. The question is whether that strategy solves your specific outbound bottleneck. Where the gap appears The gap appears when the problem is not workflow coverage, but account relevance. A sales platform can help you find contacts, enrich records, build sequences, manage replies, check deliverability, and use AI to write copy. Those are useful capabilities. But they do not automatically mean every email is grounded in a real buying reason. That distinction matters more as buyers get flooded with AI-written outbound. The old outbound question was: can we contact enough people? The current outbound question is: can we contact the right people with enough evidence that the message deserves a reply? That requires more than a first-name field and a company summary. It requires a reasoned view of the account: What pain is likely present? What is the company doing today? What status quo are they probably using? What signal suggests they may care now? What should the first message say based on that evidence? Is this lead worth contacting at all? If those questions are not answered before outreach, AI copy becomes a faster way to create generic email. This is why buyers comparing Amplemarket alternatives should avoid a feature checklist-only evaluation. A long list of modules can be useful, but the decisive issue is often upstream from sequencing. It is whether the system understands the account well enough to decide what should be sent. To be clear, this is not a claim that Amplemarket cannot support research or signals. Its official site explicitly lists intelligence, lead generation and signals, intent signals, job change alerts, competitive intelligence, social prospecting, and enrichment. The point is about buyer fit. Amplemarket’s visible positioning is a broad AI sales copilot and engagement platform. Coldreach is built around research-first qualification before outreach is written. Those are different starting assumptions. The feature checklist is not the buying decision A common mistake in AI sales tool evaluations is to create a spreadsheet with rows like enrichment, sequences, intent, inbox, deliverability, AI copy, analytics, integrations, and workflows. That checklist is useful, but incomplete. It tells you whether the product has the workflow components. It does not tell you whether the outbound motion will produce replies from the right accounts. For B2B outbound, the more useful checklist looks like this: Evaluation question Why it matters Does the workflow start with a list, or with account research? Starting with lists usually optimizes for activity. Starting with research optimizes for fit and relevance. How does the system decide why this account and why now? Generic triggers are not enough when every buyer receives AI-generated email. What evidence is used before the first message is written? Copy quality depends on input quality. Weak research creates weak personalization. Does the system qualify pain, status quo, and in-market timing? These are the variables that make outreach feel grounded instead of templated. Who owns rewriting when the AI output is generic? If reps still rewrite everything, the platform may not remove the real bottleneck. What metric proves quality? Emails sent and sequence steps completed are activity metrics. Human replies, meetings, and pipeline are closer to business outcomes. Are you replacing tool sprawl or replacing manual SDR research? These are different jobs. Do not buy one expecting it to solve the other. This is where the category split becomes obvious. If you need one system to manage more outbound workflow, evaluate a platform like Amplemarket. If you need outbound to start with better reasoning about each account, evaluate a research-first AI SDR. Research-first AI SDR comparison: how Coldreach is different Coldreach is a research-first AI SDR. We do three qualifying questions per lead - pain, status quo, in-market - and write outreach off the research. Those three questions create a different outbound motion. Pain: What business problem is likely to matter to this account? This is not generic persona pain. It has to connect to the company’s situation. Status quo: What is the account likely doing today? The best outbound often comes from understanding the current operating model, tool stack, hiring motion, messaging, market pressure, or process gap. In-market: Is there evidence that now is a reasonable time to reach out? A message sent at the wrong time is noise. A message tied to a credible buying moment has a chance. Coldreach monitors 113M+ accounts and 550M+ contacts to identify companies and people that match your ICP and buying signals. It then researches each lead, writes outreach from that research, sends through the customer’s own email infrastructure, monitors replies, and learns from performance. The performance benchmark we use externally is specific: 3.8% human reply rate, excluding auto-replies - about 10x the industry average. This is the central difference: Amplemarket is useful when you want a consolidated sales platform with engagement, signals, AI assistance, and deliverability utilities. Coldreach is useful when you want outbound to begin with account qualification and evidence-based messaging. Pricing snapshot: Amplemarket vs Coldreach Pricing should not be the only deciding factor, but it does reveal the buying motion. Plan / product Public pricing snapshot Notes Amplemarket Startup $600/month on an annual term Official visible plan for small businesses, startups, and founder-led sales teams. Includes 2 users and 27,000 contacts. Amplemarket Growth Custom Official visible packaging lists 4 users, 140,000 contacts, Dedicated CSM, Personalized Onboarding, Multichannel Sequences, AI Intent Signals, Duo Copilot, and Duo Voice. Amplemarket Elite Custom Official visible packaging lists 10 users, 400,000 contacts, Dedicated CSM, Personalized Onboarding, Multichannel Sequences, AI Intent Signals, Duo Copilot, Duo Voice, and Duo Inbox. Coldreach Starts at $899/month Research-first AI SDR that qualifies leads, writes outreach from research, sends through customer infrastructure, monitors replies, and learns. The clean way to read this: Amplemarket’s public packaging emphasizes a platform bundle with users, contacts, engagement, signals, and AI assistant surfaces. Coldreach pricing is tied to a different job: researched outbound that starts with qualification. If the budget question is “How do we consolidate multiple tools?” Amplemarket may be the more natural evaluation. If the budget question is “How do we get better replies from the accounts that matter?” Coldreach may be the more relevant comparison. Buyer decision guide Choose Amplemarket if stack consolidation is the priority. That is the cleanest fit. If your team is trying to combine prospecting, engagement, signals, enrichment, AI copy, inbox workflows, voice, social automation, and deliverability checks into one platform, Amplemarket belongs in the evaluation. It may be especially relevant if: You want a broad outbound operating system. You value multichannel engagement in the same tool as lead generation and signals. You want AI support across copy, inbox, voice, and rep workflows. You want pricing and packaging that includes contact allowances and multiple users. You are actively reducing the number of sales tools your team manages. Your team already knows its ICP, triggers, objections, and outbound messaging. Your main problem is tool overlap, not account understanding. Choose Coldreach if reply quality, account research, and in-market reasoning are the priority. Coldreach is the better fit if the team already knows that more sequences are not enough. This usually shows up in a few ways: Replies are low because the message is too generic. SDRs spend too much time researching accounts manually. AI-generated emails sound polished but not specific. The team has lists, but not enough confidence in who is actually worth contacting. Campaigns are built around volume instead of buying reasons. Leadership wants outbound pipeline, not just activity metrics. The team needs a system that learns from replies instead of only helping reps send more. Coldreach starts at the lead qualification layer. The goal is not to automate bad outbound faster. The goal is to decide who is worth contacting, understand why, then write the first message from the evidence. If your outbound problem is operational sprawl, evaluate Amplemarket. If your outbound problem is relevance, evaluate Coldreach. How to run the evaluation without fooling yourself If you are evaluating an ai sales tool Amplemarket search result, do not start with a demo checklist. Start with your bottleneck. Ask your team to bring the last 100 outbound emails that were sent to target accounts. Then ask: Did the message show a real reason for reaching out? Could the same first line have been sent to 200 similar companies? Did we know the account’s likely pain before sending? Did we know the account’s current status quo before sending? Did we have in-market evidence, or just a weak trigger? Did the email create human replies, or just opens and clicks? Did reps spend meaningful time researching and rewriting before launch? If the answer is “we mostly need cleaner workflow and consolidation,” a broad platform evaluation makes sense. If the answer is “we are sending too much generic outreach because research is shallow or manual,” then the platform checklist is not enough. You need to compare how each system decides what to say and who deserves to be contacted. That is the point of a research-first AI SDR. Bottom line Amplemarket is a credible option for teams that want an AI sales copilot and engagement platform with a wide product surface. Its official site points to a consolidated workflow across intelligence, lead generation, signals, multichannel engagement, enrichment, validation, inbox, voice, social automation, analytics, workflows, and deliverability utilities. That is valuable if your priority is stack consolidation. But outbound performance is increasingly won before the sequence starts. The decisive work is identifying the right account, understanding the current situation, finding the buying reason, and writing a message that reflects real research. Coldreach is built for that job. Coldreach is a research-first AI SDR. We do three qualifying questions per lead - pain, status quo, in-market - and write outreach off the research. 3.8% human reply rate, excluding auto-replies - about 10x the industry average. Want outbound that starts with research, not sequence templates? See how Coldreach qualifies accounts and writes the first message, then book a demo to review what that would look like for your ICP. FAQ Is Amplemarket an AI sales tool? Yes. Amplemarket’s official homepage title is “Amplemarket: AI Sales Copilot for sales teams.” Its listed product areas include Duo Copilot, Duo Copywriter, Duo Inbox, Duo Voice, lead generation and signals, multichannel engagement, enrichment, validation, and deliverability optimization. How much does Amplemarket cost? According to the official pricing page reviewed on 2026-06-22, Amplemarket’s visible Startup plan is $600/month on an annual term. It includes 2 users and 27,000 contacts. Growth and Elite are listed as custom plans, with higher user and contact allowances. What is Amplemarket best for? Amplemarket is best evaluated as a consolidated sales copilot and engagement platform. It may fit teams that want prospecting, signals, enrichment, sequences, inbox workflows, voice, social automation, and deliverability utilities in one platform. What are the best Amplemarket alternatives? The best Amplemarket alternative depends on the bottleneck. If you need stack consolidation, compare other sales engagement and sales intelligence platforms. If your bottleneck is relevance, account research, and reply quality, compare research-first AI SDRs like Coldreach. How is Coldreach different from Amplemarket? Coldreach is not trying to be a broad sales engagement suite. It is a research-first AI SDR. Coldreach qualifies each lead across pain, status quo, and in-market evidence before writing outreach. The goal is to improve reply quality by starting with account truth, not sequence volume. Does Coldreach send through my existing email infrastructure? Yes. Coldreach sends through the customer’s own email infrastructure, monitors replies, and learns from performance. This matters for teams that already have sending infrastructure and want better research, targeting, and first-message quality. When should I choose Coldreach over Amplemarket? Choose Coldreach when your main problem is that outbound is not relevant enough. If your team needs stronger account research, clearer in-market reasoning, and outreach written from evidence, Coldreach is the better fit. If your main goal is consolidating many sales workflow tools into one platform, Amplemarket may be the better category to evaluate.

title: Bali Digital Nomad Visa: Working Legally in Indonesia | Grey
summary: Can you work legally in Bali? A straight answer on Indonesia's nomad visa, Social Visa and your real options as a remote worker. Start now.
body_text: Bali has been one of the world's most popular destinations for remote workers for years. The combination of affordable living, established coworking infrastructure, warm climate, and English-friendly environment has made it a default destination for nomads. The visa situation, however, has always been more complicated than the destination's reputation suggests. Bali does not have its own visa system. Indonesia launched a Digital Nomad Visa (E33G) in 2023, but uptake has been limited. Most remote workers in Bali use a tourist visa or Social Visa, neither of which officially permits remote work. The E33G visa is the only route that explicitly allows working remotely for foreign employers. This article covers the four realistic visa options for working remotely in Bali, states clearly what each one permits and does not permit, and explains the only route that provides explicit legal authorisation for remote work. The goal is to give you accurate information so you can make an informed decision rather than a comfortable one. For a broader comparison of destinations a full list of 50 countries offering digital nomad visas . Does Bali have a digital nomad visa? Bali is a province of Indonesia, not an independent country. Indonesia's national visa system applies to Bali, Lombok, Java, and every other island. There is no Bali-specific visa. Indonesia introduced the E33G Remote Worker Visa, its formal digital nomad visa, in 2024. The E33G is a KITAS (Kartu Izin Tinggal Terbatas), a temporary stay permit, classified under the E33G visa category for remote workers employed by companies outside Indonesia. The E33G is the only visa in Indonesia's system that explicitly authorises remote work for a foreign employer while residing in Indonesia. All other commonly used visas, including the tourist Visa on Arrival, the Social or Cultural Visa (B211A), and standard business visas, do not explicitly authorise remote work. In practice, large numbers of foreigners have worked remotely in Bali on tourist visas and Social Visas for years. This was widely tolerated. The enforcement landscape changed significantly in 2025 and 2026. Bali immigration formed a dedicated enforcement task force, and deportations increased substantially, with immigration officers monitoring social media, coworking-space activity, and LinkedIn profiles as evidence for enforcement. The "open secret" that tourist visas were fine for remote work is no longer accurate to describe current conditions. Your four visa options for working remotely in Bali Visa Remote work legally permitted Duration Approximate cost Difficulty Tourist Visa on Arrival (VoA) No 30 days, extendable once to 60 days $35 per entry Low Social/Cultural Visa (B211A) No Up to 60 days, extendable to 180 days total $50 to $100 for visa; agent fees for sponsor Medium KITAS (Temporary Stay Permit) Depends on type; general KITAS for employment requires Indonesian employer 1 to 2 years $500 to $2,000+ depending on type High E33G Remote Worker Visa Yes, explicitly 12 months, non-extendable IDR 7,000,000 (~$430 USD) official fee; $600 to $1,000 with agent and KITAS processing Medium Tourist Visa on Arrival (VoA) Available to citizens of most countries on arrival at major Indonesian airports and seaports. Valid for 30 days, extendable once for a further 30 days at an immigration office. No advance application required. The VoA does not permit remote work for a foreign employer. It is a leisure and short-stay visa. Many remote workers use it anyway. Enforcement risk has increased in 2026, with immigration specifically targeting foreigners working on tourist visas. Social/Cultural Visa (B211A) Requires an Indonesian sponsor, a cultural institution, language school, or individual, to provide a letter of sponsorship. The B211A allows stays of up to 60 days, extendable multiple times to a maximum of 180 days total. It does not explicitly permit remote work. B211A enforcement increased in 2025 and 2026, with deportations specifically citing remote workers on social visas. The B211A remains popular among nomads on longer Bali stays, but it carries a higher enforcement risk than before. KITAS (Temporary Stay Permit) The general KITAS is a residency permit for people with legitimate reasons to live in Indonesia long-term, including employment with an Indonesian company, marriage to an Indonesian citizen, or investment. An employment KITAS requires an Indonesian employer and work permit, which is not relevant for remote workers employed abroad. The E33G is technically classified as a KITAS variant, specifically the E33G Remote Worker KITAS. This is the relevant version for digital nomads. E33G Remote Worker Visa The only visa in Indonesia's system that explicitly authorises remote work for a foreign employer while residing in Indonesia. Introduced in 2024, it is valid for 12 months, allows multiple entries, and does not require an Indonesian sponsor. Indonesia E33G digital nomad visa: requirements Confirm the current requirements from Indonesia's Directorate General of Immigration at imigrasi.go.id before applying, as they are subject to change. Employment type: You must be employed by a company registered outside Indonesia. The E33G is designed for remote employees, not freelancers. Freelancers with clients outside Indonesia sit in a grey area; consult a licensed Indonesian immigration agent before applying if your income is freelance-based. Minimum annual income: $60,000 per year, or the equivalent in foreign currency, from a foreign employer or clients Bank account balance: Minimum $2,000 USD in a bank account for three consecutive months prior to application Passport validity: At least 18 months of remaining validity and three blank pages. Employment contract: A valid employment contract with a non-Indonesian company confirming a remote work arrangement. Health insurance: Valid health insurance covering Indonesia Criminal record: Clean background check Restricted nationalities: Citizens of certain countries are not eligible; verify the current exclusion list on the official Indonesian immigration website The E33G does not permit any income-generating work for Indonesian companies or clients. Even consulting for a local business, accepting payment from an Indonesian entity, or providing services to someone who pays you from Indonesia violates the visa terms. How to apply for the E33G visa: step by step Confirm eligibility. Verify your income meets the $60,000 annual threshold, your employer is registered outside Indonesia, and your nationality is not on the restricted list. If you are self-employed or freelance, consult an immigration agent before proceeding. Gather your documents. Passport (all pages), employment contract confirming remote work with a non-Indonesian company, three to six months of bank statements demonstrating consistent income above the threshold, health insurance certificate covering Indonesia, and a criminal background check from your home country. Choose your application route. Applications can be submitted at an Indonesian embassy or consulate in your home country. Some applicants use licensed Indonesian immigration agents who handle the KITAS processing on arrival. The official fee at the consulate is IDR 7,000,000, approximately $430 USD. Total costs, including KITAS card processing and agent fees, typically run from $600 to $1,000. Submit the application and pay the fee. Fees are non-refundable regardless of outcome as of May 2025 enforcement changes. Wait for processing. Processing typically takes 7 to 14 working days. Your application may be approved or may require additional documents. Enter Indonesia and activate the permit. Enter through an approved port of entry. The E33G sticker is placed in your passport. Complete KITAS card processing at the immigration office in your area of residence in Indonesia, typically within 14 days of arrival. Note: you must enter Indonesia within 90 days of the visa issuance date, or the visa will become void. See the must-haves for digital nomads before your move. Costs, practical realities and managing money in Bali Visa cost: IDR 7,000,000 (~$430 USD) official fee, plus an additional $200 to $600 for agent and KITAS card processing. Total first-year cost: $600 to $1,000 depending on how you apply. Cost of living in Bali: Monthly costs vary significantly by lifestyle and area. A realistic mid-range budget covers $400 to $700 for a one-bedroom villa, $200 to $400 for food (a mix of local warungs and occasional restaurants), $100 to $200 for a coworking membership, and $50 to $100 for transport. A comfortable monthly budget runs $1,000 to $2,000, considerably less than most Western cities. Tax position: Staying in Indonesia for more than 183 days in a calendar year triggers Indonesian tax residency under domestic law, which makes worldwide income potentially taxable in Indonesia. Foreign-sourced income remitted to Indonesia may also be subject to tax depending on the bilateral tax treaty between Indonesia and your home country. Many E33G holders plan their annual stay to remain below 183 days in a given calendar year to reduce this exposure. The interaction between home country tax obligations and Indonesian tax residency is complex. Consult a cross-border tax adviser before making long-term plans. Internet: Bali's internet infrastructure is adequate for most remote work in major nomad hubs including Canggu, Seminyak, Ubud, and Sanur. Coworking spaces reliably offer 50 to 100 Mbps. Residential connections are more variable. Most nomads use a combination of home internet and coworking access. Managing USD earnings while spending in IDR: Most digital nomads in Bali earn in USD, GBP, or EUR and spend in Indonesian rupiah. Converting at Bali's money changers produces reasonable rates, but doing large conversions repeatedly adds up. Grey provides multi-currency accounts where you can hold USD or EUR income and use a Grey virtual debit card for daily expenses, avoiding the 2% to 3% foreign transaction fee that standard debit cards add to every IDR charge. Open a Grey account before you head to Bali. Hold USD, GBP and EUR in one place and spend in IDR locally. Frequently asked questions Can I work remotely in Bali on a tourist visa? Legally, no. The Tourist Visa on Arrival does not authorise remote work for a foreign employer. Enforcement of this rule increased significantly in 2025 and 2026, with Bali immigration conducting active operations in popular nomad areas, including Canggu and Seminyak, and using social media monitoring and LinkedIn activity as evidence of enforcement. The risk of working on a tourist visa in Bali is meaningfully higher in 2026 than it was in the past. What is the Indonesia E33G digital nomad visa? The E33G Remote Worker Visa is a temporary stay permit (KITAS) launched by Indonesia in 2024. It is the only visa in Indonesia's system that explicitly authorises remote work for a foreign employer while residing in Indonesia. It is valid for 12 months, allows multiple entries, and requires a minimum annual income of $60,000 from non-Indonesian sources. It does not permit work for Indonesian companies or clients. How much does it cost to live in Bali as a digital nomad? A comfortable mid-range monthly budget runs $1,000 to $2,000 depending on accommodation choice, lifestyle, and how much you eat out at tourist-priced restaurants versus local warungs. Accommodation is the largest variable: a basic room in a guesthouse costs $300 to $500 per month, while a private villa with pool access in Canggu or Seminyak costs $700 to $2,000 depending on size and season. Do I pay tax in Indonesia if I work remotely in Bali? Staying in Indonesia for more than 183 days in a calendar year triggers Indonesian tax residency, which makes worldwide income potentially subject to Indonesian tax. Foreign-sourced income that is not remitted to Indonesia is generally not taxed under most circumstances, but the rules depend on the specific bilateral tax treaty between Indonesia and your home country. Consult a qualified tax professional before planning an extended stay. How long can I stay in Bali as a digital nomad? For a Tourist Visa on Arrival, the maximum stay is 60 days (a 30-day initial visa plus one 30-day extension). On a B211A Social Visa, up to 180 days total across extensions. On the E33G Remote Worker Visa, 12 months with multiple entries. After 12 months on the E33G visa, the visa is non-extendable, and the holder must leave Indonesia and reapply from outside Indonesia. Can I get internet fast enough to work remotely in Bali? Yes, in the major nomad hubs. Coworking spaces in Canggu, Seminyak, Ubud, and Sanur consistently offer 50-100 Mbps connections with backup options. Residential internet is more variable, and older properties in less-developed areas may have slower or less reliable connections. For work requiring stable video calls and cloud uploads, coworking is the most reliable option. Mobile data from Telkomsel or XL Axiata provides a usable backup connection.

title: What's new in Git 2.55.0?
summary: Learn about the new features and changes in Git 2.55, including a new git-history(1) fixup command, an fsmonitor daemon for Linux, pushing to remote groups, and more.
body_text: The Git project recently released Git 2.55.0 . Let's look at a few notable highlights from this release, which includes contributions from the Git team at GitLab. What's covered: git-history(1) learns fixup fsmonitor daemon for Linux git push to a remote group Limiting git log --graph lane width Evolution of Rust in the Git codebase Faster git-grep(1) and git-cherry(1) in partial clones git-history(1) learns fixup In our highlights of Git 2.54.0 , we covered the introduction of git-history(1) . In 2.55.0, a new subcommand for this tool was added: fixup . Imagine you've made some changes and you want to amend those changes into an existing commit. The most common approach to this is to create a fixup commit and autosquash it with git-rebase(1) : git commit --fixup= < commit-id > git rebase -i --autosquash < commit-i d > ^ Doing this in two steps is clumsy, especially because it requires an interactive rebase. Instead you can use the git-history(1) fixup command: git history fixup < commit-i d > This takes the staged changes and amends them into the given commit. As an added bonus, because you're using git-history(1), all other local branches that contain the fixed-up commit are updated as well. So when working with stacked branches, fixup-ing a commit in the stack will automatically rebase all related branches. This feature was implemented by Patrick Steinhardt . fsmonitor daemon for Linux When working with large monorepos, git-status(1) can be slow to determine what changed in the local worktree because Git would need to traverse the whole working tree to see which files are modified. To speed up this process, in January 2018 a setting core.fsmonitor was added in Git 2.16. Back then, you had to provide your own tool (like Watchman ). When this was configured, this tool runs in the background and monitors changes on the file system. This informs Git that a file was touched and Git then verifies whether the file was modified and updates the cached status. Then whenever the user calls git-status(1), it can simply return the cached status. In April 2022, the setting core.fsmonitor was changed to accept a boolean value. When this setting is set to true , a daemon built-in into Git is used and no more third-party tool is needed. But this filesystem monitor was only implemented for Windows and macOS, support for GNU/Linux did not yet exist. This changes in Git 2.55, where support for Linux has been added, too. To achieve this, inotify(7) is used. inotify(7) was chosen over fanotify(7) because fanotify(7) requires elevated privileges. This comes with a small caveat though, the fsmonitor needs to put a watcher on each and every directory in the repository. In a large repo you might hit the limit of inotify watches ( fs.inotify.max_user_watches ), which you may need to raise. These changes were submitted by Paul Tarjan based on work by Eric DeCosta and Marziyeh Esipreh . git push to a remote group Quite some time ago git-fetch(1) learned to fetch from a group of remotes. The following command configures a group of remotes: git config set remotes.forks "origin upstream" When this is set up, you can git-fetch(1) from this "forks" group, and then all the remotes in that list are fetched from. This can be useful when you want to get the updates from a set of remotes in one go. git-push(1) , however, was not able to use remote groups. In Git 2.55, this gap is closed and git-push(1) now accepts a remote group too. For example if you want to push the main branch to the group mentioned above: git push forks main Similar as with git-fetch(1), this command pushes the specified refs to each of the remotes in the group. Each remote is pushed independently and honors its own remote.<name>.push mapping and mirror settings. This feature was submitted by Usman Akinyemi , suggested by Junio C Hamano . Limiting git log --graph lane width The --graph option of git-log(1) draws an ASCII representation of the commit history. In a repository with many active contributors this graph can grow very wide. For example, on the git.git repository this graph grows nine lanes wide after only 30 commits: * 26d8d94e94 A few more topics before -rc2 * 02bb39c5cb Merge branch 'js/objects-larger-than-4gb-on-windows-more' |\ | * c6a4629e32 odb: use size_t for object_info.sizep and the size APIs | * 7a3a78cc76 packfile,delta: drop the `cast_size_t_to_ulong()` wrappers | * 188bac14f7 pack-objects: use size_t for in-core object sizes | * 2d83cc3f84 packfile: widen unpack_entry()'s size out-parameter to size_t | * 1d43315b31 pack-objects(check_pack_inflate()): use size_t instead of unsigned long | * 33afe87338 patch-delta: use size_t for sizes | * 8ea69373a4 compat/msvc: use _chsize_s for ftruncate * | 8cf57cbec4 Merge branch 'kw/gitattributes-typofix' |\ \ | * | accumulator * | | | | 619931f561 Merge branch 'dl/posix-unused-warning-clang' |\ \ \ \ \ | * | | | | cf48887610 compat/posix.h: simplify GIT_GNUC_PREREQ() comparison | * | | | | ffd45926dc the commit from where the branch was created. This pushes the commit messages off to the right, making it harder to read. Especially when the terminal screen width is reached, this becomes unusable. Git 2.55 adds a new --graph-lane-limit=<n> option to limit the number of lanes that are drawn. Any lanes beyond the limit are replaced with a ~ truncation mark, so it stays obvious that the graph was trimmed: git log --graph --graph-lane-limit=5 Using this option for the same 30 commits as
